verses.1: Al-Mizan takes the address to the Prophet in the customary sense of addressing a community through its leader, not as an ellipsis requiring him to tell the community. Divorce for the prescribed time means initiating divorce at the beginning of the wife’s ʿiddah: in a non-menstruating cycle in which intercourse has not occurred, then counting the cycles until it ends. During that period she has maintenance and shelter, while the husband may return to her. Expelling her, or her leaving, is forbidden; the homes are called theirs because they live in them. The exception is manifest indecency, such as adultery, obscenity, or, according to narrations from the Imams, harassment of the household. These divorce rules are God’s limits, whose breach is disobedience and self-wronging; reconciliation may yet change the husband’s heart.
verses.2: Al-Mizan understands reaching the prescribed time as nearing the end of the ʿiddah. Retaining the wife means returning to her, while separating means allowing her to complete it; either course must be maʿrūf, the legally ordained custom that observes her rights. Two just companions are to witness the divorce and testify uprightly for God. The admonition covers the divine ordinances, piety, sincere testimony, and the ban on transgressing God’s limits: it calls believers to truth and the removal of falsehood, and hints that altering those ordinances takes one outside faith. Taqwā is avoiding prohibitions, observing the limits and sharīʿah, which accords with human nature and opens a way through life’s hardships toward happiness here and hereafter.
verses.3: Al-Mizan first reads unexpected sustenance in the divorce context as a spouse, wealth, and the requirements of a wholesome, pure life, assuring the faithful that obedience to God’s limits does not bring poverty. Trust in God means setting aside one’s desire for His will and living by His religion; He suffices for the good life and natural happiness people truly seek, not their false imaginations. God is the ultimate cause: apparent causes act only by His grant and permission, while His will is unimpeded and every created thing is measured, unlike God Himself. Read beyond the immediate context, true taqwā—grounded in knowing God’s names and attributes—brings a servant’s will into the divine will and makes him see his faculties as God’s alone. This is God’s wilāyah, freeing him from reliance on apparent causes and from shirk, and providing both unanticipated material means and enduring spiritual sustenance. The awliyāʾ receive this fully; ordinary believers receive according to their sincerity, faith, and deeds, and rise toward it by repentance from hidden shirk.
verses.4: Al-Mizan defines irtiyāb as uncertainty about whether menstruation will occur, whether through age or another cause. Women who no longer expect menstruation, or are uncertain about it, observe a three-month ʿiddah; so do women of menstruating age who have not menstruated. A pregnant woman’s ʿiddah ends with delivery. Taqwā brings ease in the hardships one faces; some interpret that ease as worldly and otherworldly, either immediate relief or compensation in the hereafter.
verses.5: Al-Mizan identifies God’s command with the divorce and ʿiddah rulings just given. Carrying them out is part of taqwā, alongside avoiding what is forbidden, and therefore entails not neglecting them. God’s removal of evil means forgiveness for lesser sins; greater transgressions remain. Read with the distinction between avoiding major sins and the covering of misdeeds, the commentary concludes that violating the revealed divorce and waiting-period rules is unquestionably a major sin, not a fault overlooked through piety.
verses.6: Al-Mizan takes min wujdikum to require lodging divorced women according to a husband’s ability and wealth, whether he is rich or poor. He must not injure them by making lodging, clothing, or upkeep burdensome. A pregnant woman is supported until delivery, and if she nurses the child she is paid, as this is part of the father’s support owed to the child. The parents must consult one another and agree according to custom, protecting the father from excessive expense, the mother from deprivation, and the child from loss of a full nursing period. If their demands impose hardship and they cannot agree, the father may employ another woman, not the mother, to nurse the child.
verses.7: Al-Mizan directs the wealthy to spend generously on divorced women nursing their children, and the poor to provide from what God has given them. Required upkeep is proportionate to means: God does not impose a burden beyond what He has granted. The promise that ease follows difficulty encourages and reassures those meeting this obligation.
verses.8: Al-Mizan reads qaryah as its people, ʿutuw as recalcitrance in obedience akin to arrogance, and nukr as an unprecedented, terrible punishment. Their rebellion included shirk, denial of the messengers’ call, abandonment of God’s ordinances, and rejection of the messengers’ wilāyah. The severe accounting is worldly, not an already-certain future accounting: afflictions religiously count as consequences of deeds, though God pardons much, while the insolent are severely censured, punished in unheard-of ways, and eradicated. The alternative reading of the past tense as future reckoning is rejected. The shift from third person to first person underscores the enormity of this punishment.
verses.9: Al-Mizan takes amrahā to mean the people’s rebellion and arrogance: they tasted the consequence of their insolence, ending in loss, as though they had exchanged obedience for haughtiness.
verses.10: Al-Mizan distinguishes the severe chastisement prepared hereafter from the worldly accounting and loss described previously. Its unlinked wording answers the implied question of what their perdition means. Believing people of understanding are therefore warned to acquire taqwā rather than rebel against God’s command; their intellects, alerted by the repeated ruin of insolent peoples, should turn them from arrogance. The revealed reminder tells them what is for and against them and guides them to truth and the straight path.
verses.11: Al-Mizan understands the Messenger as an apposition or substitute for dhikr, so that the reminder is Muḥammad, who reminds people of God and His signs and calls to the true religion. Sending him means appointing him from the unseen and making his messengership known, not necessarily sending him physically from heaven. The reading that identifies him as Gabriel conflicts with the apparent sense of the one who recites God’s clear communications, though an elided ‘We sent a messenger’ remains possible, with dhikr then referring to the Qur’an, its rulings, or wisdom. The Messenger brings believers who do good from darkness to light; their goodly sustenance includes faith and righteous deeds in this world and the Garden hereafter, rather than only the Garden as some say.
verses.12: Al-Mizan says this creation statement confirms the preceding lordship, messenger, reminder, punishment, and reward, because God is all-powerful and all-knowing. ‘Of the earth like them’ apparently means seven earths corresponding in number to the seven heavens; their nature is left among possibilities such as separate spheres, concentric layers, or climatic zones. It may also refer to the human being, formed from earth with a heavenly soul. The descending amr is the unrestricted creative command, passing through the heavens to the earthly realm and manifesting creation, effects, provision, death, life, honour, and humiliation; restricting it to sharīʿah rulings revealed through angels does not fit the verse’s conclusion. Contemplating this creation and command establishes God’s power and encompassing knowledge, and should make thoughtful believers fear opposition to the One who rewards obedience and punishes rebellion.
